content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review:
This paper employed fuzz testing approach to generate black-box adversarial examples. In general, the fuzz testing is new to the adversarial attack area to the best of reviewer's knowledge. One difference with the existing black-box attack generation methods is that AdvFuzzer walks from a source image to a guidance image rather than starting from a targeted image. However, I still have concerns about this submission. 

1) Figure 1 is not clear. Please highlight AdvFuzzer and LocalFuzzer and clarify the meaning of the color and symbols.

2) The algorithm presentation is poor. It makes the current technical contributions unclear. What is the challenge when applying fuzz testing to adversarial example generation? And what are technical contributions induced by this new challenge?

3) Some experiments are unclear to me. 
3.1) The lack of ImageNet results is a weak point. 
3.2) What is the computational complexity of the proposed fuzzing-based approach? Having a comparison on computation time might be helpful.
3.3) The second row of Figure 2 seemingly implies that fuzzing attacks lead to much higher L_inf distortion. Right? Is there any comparison under L_inf  metric? This observation also holds in Table 1 and 2 (small L_0 but large L_2). Thus, I wonder if the reduced query number is at the cost of a significant increase of L_inf norm. For a fair comparison, it might need to add L_inf constraint such that all methods have similar pixel-level perturbation tolerance. E.g., one related work on black-box soft-label/hard-label attack https://arxiv.org/pdf/1907.11684.pdf

Thus, my initial rating is weak reject. 

############### Post-feedback ############
Thanks for the detailed response. My concerns on 1) and 2) have been addressed. However, my concern on ImageNet results remains. 

It is difficult to get an idea on how well the proposed algorithm performs in the absence of baseline in Table 7  " Average, Median, and Standard Deviation Results for Untargeted Attacks on ImageNet using Fuzzing attacks". 


Thus, I keep my score intact.

content.title: Responses to Reviewer 1
content.comment:
Many thanks for your comments.  Please see whether our responses address some of your concerns:

1. We revised Figure 1.  We also added the legends to it and refined its caption.

2. In Section 3.1, we added that “The main challenge of applying fuzz testing to adversarial example generation is on exploring the gigantic search space. Theoretically, a fuzzer is able to explore the entire search space, but this is computationally infeasible. We address this challenge by using a guidance image and certain guidance strategy to improve the attack efficiency, i.e., fewer queries.”

We had the sentences here and there in our original submission on the details of the guidance strategy together with the description of the two algorithms.  Perhaps our response to Reviewer 3 could answer your question regarding “technical contributions induced by this new challenge”.  We paste the response here for your convenience:

In AdvFuzzer, starting from the source image, each main step is taken by changing one pixel toward the guidance image (Algorithm 1, lines 4-5).  This step is guided by the L0 strategy as described in the paper and is obviously not random.  

In LocalFuzzer, only one pixel in the seed image is mutated (Algorithm 2, line 10) as described in the paper. This step is random on purpose because we want to leverage the randomness advantage of fuzz testing.

The walk_back fuzzer mutates an image by “randomly changing some pixel values of a current image closer or directly to that of the source image” as described in the paper.  This step is random on the selection of pixels but guided on value changes.

In essence, we considered both certain guidances and some randomness in our overall approach.  Lacking either of them would result in poor performance than what we can achieve at this moment.  However, we did/do not claim our detailed steps as optimal.  On the contrary, we show the feasibility of the fuzzing approach and suggested at the end of the paper that “potential ways for improvement could be a better guidance strategy in the main direction selection, a refined seed selection process, a refined mutation function, etc .”.

3. Regarding the experiments:
3.1 Experiments on ImageNet are very timing consuming. We hope to provide some initial evidence in our upcoming revision.

3.2 As described in our original submission, in AdvFuzzer (Algorithm 1), “the while loop ends whenever a successful example is found or the number of steps reaches the maximum number of steps which is the L0 distance between the source image and the guidance image”; in LocalFuzzer, the constant value fuzzer_level “controls the total number of mutated images to be generated”.  So overall, the time complexity of AdvFuzzer is roughly linear to the fuzzer_level (because the image size and correspondingly the maximum L0 distance is a constant, and the time of a single query to a given black-box model can be considered as a constant too).

Unfortunately we didn’t record the overall generation time in our experiments (as we did not see such information in Boundary and OPT papers). The actual time taken depends on the system resources available for each run. We hope to provide some micro-level measurement results in our upcoming revision.

3.3 Yes you are correct that Linf values are high in our fuzzing attacks.  We thought that was obvious (as our attacks have lower L0 but higher L2 values) so we did not add Linf results in our original submission.  We now added Linf results in the corresponding tables.  Adding Linf constraint is a very good suggestion, and may help reduce both Linf and L2 distances.  We are reading the black-box soft-label/hard-label attack paper that you recommended, and will find a place to cite it in our upcoming revision.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2545
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper proposes a fuzzing technique to mutate images in a black-box manner for realizing targeted and un-targeted attacks. The authors evaluate the effectiveness of their technique on MNIST and CIFAR-10 dataset.

+The paper is generally well-written and easy to follow. Fuzzing is a well-explored area in Software Engineering and this paper shows the potential of fuzzing for adversarial attacks. 

- My main concern of this paper is the results (Section 4). Though for the untargeted attack on  MNIST dataset the proposed technique performs well, its performance is not that satisfactory, especially for CIFAR-10. For an untargeted attack (Table-1) though L0 is significantly low compared to baseline attacks, L2 is increased. This is even worse for Targeted attacks (Table 2)----both reported L0 and L2 loss are greater than C&W L0 attack. 

- What is the justification of using Fuzzing 300 and 500 settings, as their number of queries almost match with Opt Attack? 

- The evaluation tasks for BlackBox attacks should be performed on black-box scenarios such as google cloud API and Amazon API settings. Instead, the authors use simple white-box settings like mnist, cifar10.

-	“Note that due to the randomness of our fuzzing attacks, the results could vary in a certain range from run to run.” --- How much is this variation?

- The paper exceeds 8 page page-limit.

- In the methodology section, it is not clear to me how many pixels are mutated per step? It apparently looks like one pixel is selected per step without any guidance. This is almost like a simple brute force approach.

content.title: Responses to Reviewer 3
content.comment:
Many thanks for your comments.  Please see whether our responses address some of your concerns:

1. Regarding your comments on L2 distance, our opinion is that it could be the goal of many adversarial example generation algorithms, but is not necessarily the most important goal of real-world attackers.  Please read our common response to all reviewers for a more detailed discussion.

2. Fuzzing 300 and 500 settings are for different levels of small LocalFuzzer sizes. Although LocalFuzzer size 300 or 500 takes more queries than LocalFuzzer size 100, a larger fuzzing size allows LocalFuzzer to explore the local space with a finer granularity. With some better guidance strategy, a larger fuzzing size could potentially lead to less distortion.  We added these two settings to evaluate the effect of LocalFuzzer size.

3. In our experiments, we followed what the authors of Boundary and OPT attacks did, so we did not use Cloud APIs either.  Using Google Cloud APIs and Amazon APIs could be valuable, and we are investigating the cost as well as experimental design.

4. Regarding the variation corresponding to the untargeted and targeted attacks in Table 1 and Table 2, we have added median distance value and number of query results in Table 5 and Table 6 of Appendix for untargeted and targeted attacks, respectively.

5. In AdvFuzzer, starting from the source image, each main step is taken by changing one pixel toward the guidance image (Algorithm 1, lines 4-5).  This step is guided by the L0 strategy as described in the paper and is obviously not random.  

In LocalFuzzer, only one pixel in the seed image is mutated (Algorithm 2, line 10) as described in the paper. This step is random on purpose because we want to leverage the randomness advantage of fuzz testing.

The walk_back fuzzer mutates an image by “randomly changing some pixel values of a current image closer or directly to that of the source image” as described in the paper.  This step is random on the selection of pixels but guided on value changes.

In essence, we considered both certain guidances and some randomness in our overall approach.  Lacking either of them would result in poor performance than what we can achieve at this moment.  However, we did/do not claim our detailed steps as optimal.  On the contrary, we show the feasibility, benefits, and current limitations of our fuzzing approach, and suggested at the end of the paper that “potential ways for improvement could be a better guidance strategy in the main direction selection, a refined seed selection process, a refined mutation function, etc .”.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper proposes a new decision based attack algorithm. Given a targeted example and original example, the algorithm gradually check samples on this path with some local noise randomly added. The authors show that their approach can get better L_0 perturbation on MNIST and CIFAR-10. 

Although the algorithm is novel, there are several weaknesses in both algorithm design and experimental evaluation. 

Experimental comparisons: 
1. From the tables, the authors show improved L0 perturbation but with much worse L2 perturbation, which was the focus in both Boundary and OPT attack. Therefore it's not very convincing that the proposed method can improve the quality of adversarial example on standard L2 or even Linfty, L1 perturbations. As mentioned in the first paragraph of section 3.2, the authors mentioned that their method can also be applied to L2 perturbation, so a more fair comparison would be trying L2 version of Fussing-based attack and comparing it with Boundary and OPT attacks. 

From Figure 2 we can clearly observe perturbations, and comparing with the quality we got using L2 perturbation based algorithms (Boundary and OPT attack), I feel the proposed algorithm leads to human-perceptible perturbations. 

2. I am quite concern about whether AdvFuzzer is sensitive to the target image, since it only samples points on the path toward one target image, but the goal of either targeted or untargeted attack is not to perturb toward a particular target image, but to find the minimum perturbation that changes label. So, how do you select the target image? Is the algorithm sensitive to this selection?

3. No experiments on ImageNet (note that both Boundary and OPT attacks have been tested on ImageNet). 

Regarding the algorithm : 
4. The algorithm might have huge memory requirement since the set Sadv keeps growing. What's the max size of Sadv set in your experiments?

content.title: Responses to Reviewer 2
content.comment:
Many thanks for your comments.  Please see whether our responses address some of your concerns:

1. We did/do not claim that our current version AdvFuzzer improves L2 over Boundary and OPT attacks.  They are closely related black-box attacks, so we simply compared our results with theirs and acknowledged the limitations of our current version AdvFuzzer from the L2 distance perspective.  However, we showed that our LocalFuzzer can “immediately generate more successful adversarial examples even with smaller L2 distance”, this is true for the examples of Boundary and OPT as shown in our original submission and also true for the examples of C&W L0 and L2 attacks.  Our intention was/is not on beating Boundary and OPT attacks; instead, we are more interested in whether and how fuzzing techniques can be used in generating adversarial examples.  Currently we are working on using some L2 strategy to improve human perception.

2. Our current version AdvFuzzer uses any randomly selected target image as guidance for the source image to walk across the decision boundary. We need to leverage some information from the target class space to guide this process especially for the targeted attacks. For simplicity, in each run we only randomly selected one image from the target class space as the guidance. Note that even for Boundary and Opt attacks, they also need to use an initial start point (image) in the target class space to walk toward the source class space.

Although many algorithms aim to minimize L2, it does not mean that L2 minimization is the main goal for all attackers.  Please read our common response to all reviewers for a more detailed discussion.

3. Experiments on ImageNet are very timing consuming. We hope to provide some initial evidence in our upcoming revision.

4. Set Sadv does not keep growing because once we find a successful example, the condition at line 3 in Algorithm 1 becomes false and the loop terminates. The max size of Sadv is the size of small or medium LocalFuzzer level.  In most cases, successful examples are first identified from the small level LocalFuzzer.  This is because when the main step is not reaching the decision boundary yet, LocalFuzzer is capable of finding adversarial examples across the boundary. We observed that the Sadv size is mostly 20-50% of the small LocalFuzzer size (which is 100, 300, or 500 in experiments of Section 4.1, and 100, 1000, or 5000 in experiments of Section 4.2).

content.title: Common response to all reviewers
content.comment:
Dear Reviewers,

We appreciate the suggestions and comments from all of you. We updated the paper by addressing some comments including (1) Figure 1 revision and clarification, (2) Linf results, (3) challenges when applying fuzz testing and corresponding contributions, and (4) median & standard deviation results. We also added the bulk generation results based on the adversarial examples of white-box C&W L0 and L2 attacks, showing that LocalFuzzer is still very useful.  We are addressing some other comments and will upload another revision by the due date.

In the Conclusion and Discussion section of our original submission, we highlighted that “The experimental results demonstrated that our fuzzing attacks are feasible and effective. Moreover, LocalFuzzer has the bulk successful example generation capability and distance refinement capability on adversarial examples generated from different attack methods.”;  we acknowledged that “one limitation of our attacks is that they sacrifice the L2 distance to a small extent.”; we also suggested that “potential ways for improvement could be a better guidance strategy in the main direction selection, a refined seed selection process, a refined mutation function, etc .”.

We thank the reviewers for commenting on the novelty of our approach.  The first work seems to be always hard and there are many potentials for improvement.  We reply to your other comments below your original messages. 

Here, we want to add a common response that we have some different opinions regarding minimizing the L2 distance - it could be the goal of many adversarial example generation algorithms, but is not necessarily the most important goal of real-world attackers.  In other words, attackers’ adversarial examples need not be “perfect” (in terms of L2 distance).  Whatever adversarial examples that are reasonably good (e.g., most humans can still recognize as the source class but models will be fooled) can be used by attackers.   It is common in many types of real-world attacks that techniques need not be perfect.  For example, in phishing attacks,  super simple spoofed login webpages are still widely used by attackers.

Indeed, we also highlighted in our original submission that “LocalFuzzer itself can be an independent and useful tool to augment many adversarial example generation algorithms.”  We showed that the “optimized” adversarial examples from Boundary attack and Opt attack can further be refined, i.e., reducing their L2 distances.  We added in this revision that this capability of LocalFuzzer is also true on the adversarial examples generated by white-box attacks such as C&W L0 and L2 attacks.

Sincerely,
Authors.
